items.caption: This instance represents ONE Comet WiFi thermostat. It is matched via its MAC address; the topics are derived from it and do not need to be entered.

The values appear as soon as the device reports in on its own. After creating the instance this can take anywhere from a few minutes to several hours — the thermostats only rarely send anything in their power-saving mode.

⚠️  A setpoint set here is not permanent: the weekly schedule in the device keeps running and overwrites it at the next switching point — and so does the manufacturer's app. This is the device's behaviour, not a fault of the module.

Only registers with a confirmed meaning are kept as variables. Weekly schedule, holiday, key lock, temperature offset and the device information (model, firmware, IP, Wi-Fi) are decoded. Still open are the sensitivity of the ventilation detection and two registers with no recognisable counterpart — if you switch on raw data capture and archive it, you help with decoding them.
This instance must be placed under an MQTT Client (or MQTT Server) that is connected to the thermostats' broker.

items.name: MAC
items.caption: MAC address
Where do I get the MAC address?

popup.caption: Where do I get the MAC address?

items.caption: Twelve hex characters without separators, e.g. A1B2C3D4E5F6. The configurator enters it automatically when creating the instance.
By hand you can find it in the broker's log: the last six characters are part of the device's client ID (structure da16x02 + user name + last three MAC bytes).

items.name: MQTTUser
items.caption: MQTT user
What is the MQTT user?
The eight-character account identifier shared by all Comet WiFi devices of one account. It is different for every user — the default is only an example.
It can be read from a device's MQTT connection setup (port 1883 is unencrypted), see the README.

items.name: ForceManualOnSet
items.caption: Switch to manual mode when a setpoint is set

Without this switch a setpoint only holds until the next switching point: the weekly schedule in the device then takes over again. For automations from within Symcon the switch is therefore almost always wanted.

The device's scale runs from "Off" through 8.0–28.0 °C up to "On". The two end stops are not temperatures but valve fully closed (7.5) and fully open (28.5) — exactly as the display shows it. The default values cover this scale completely; a restriction only makes sense if you deliberately do not want to reach the end stops.

items.name: BatteryDecode
items.caption: Read battery value as
The encoding of the battery value is not confirmed. If the display shows implausible values, switch it here.

⚠️  Comet WiFi runs on batteries. Every query wakes the device. After a comparable redirection, battery failure within about two weeks was reported in the ioBroker community. When in doubt, leave it at 0 (off) — the devices report in on their own.

items.name: PollInterval
items.caption: Active query every … minutes (0 = off)

⚠️  At 0 it stays that way: these thermostats send practically nothing on their own. They report when they connect and when they are asked — otherwise not. Without active polling the values in Symcon can therefore be many hours old. That is not a fault but the price of sparing the batteries.

items.name: TimeoutMinutes
items.caption: Report as unreachable after … minutes without a message

items.name: ProbeAfterLoss
items.caption: Ask once after a connection loss

The broker's disconnect notice only says that a session ended — not that the device is gone. It also comes when the same device logs in again, and in bulk for all devices when the broker briefly drops out. Without asking, "unreachable" would then stay forever. Only the temperatures are requested; if the device really is gone, the request lapses without consequences.
For further development of the protocol. Not needed in everyday use.

items.name: RawRegisters
items.caption: Keep raw data of all unknown registers as variables

These five carry the same value across ten devices checked and can therefore represent neither a state nor a setting — presumably states passed through from the Wi-Fi chip. They are normally not created.

items.name: RawSilentRegisters
items.caption: Also capture the registers proven to be empty (B4, B5, B7, BB, BC)
Creates a text variable for each unknown register. Anyone who archives these provides the material needed to decode the weekly schedule, window detection and the options bit field after the fact.

items.name: DebugUnknown
items.caption: Write unknown registers to the debug window

The weekly schedule runs in the thermostat, not in Symcon. If the device's clock is wrong, every switching point is shifted by the same amount — a setback at 21:00 with a 40-minute lead already arrives at 20:20.

Setting the clock is confirmed on the device: the value written comes back unchanged and the deviation drops to zero. The date is applied as well. After setting, the clock is read back — so the display updates by itself.

items.name: ClockWarnMinutes
items.caption: Warn from a deviation of
0 switches the warning off.

items.name: ClockSyncDays
items.caption: Adjust the clock automatically every

0 leaves it alone — that is the default, because every adjustment wakes a battery-powered device. When switched on, the clock is only set if the deviation is above the warning threshold; and the timing is offset per device, so that ten thermostats do not wake up at the same moment.

After a module update, Symcon does not always apply an instance's settings by itself. The only other way is to change something in the form and change it back — only then does "Apply" become clickable at all. This button saves you that.
⚠️  Acts on the saved settings. Anything you changed above but have not applied yet is lost.
This is harmless for the devices: applying sends nothing and therefore does not wake any battery.
